title: Predicting equilibrium distributions for molecular systems with deep learning

nodes.text: Distributional Graphormer (DiG) is a deep learning framework that uses a diffusion process implemented with the Graphormer architecture to transform a simple distribution into the equilibrium distribution of a molecular system, conditioned on a descriptor such as a chemical graph or protein sequence.
nodes.evidence: we introduce a deep learning framework, called Distributional Graphormer (DiG), in an attempt to predict the equilibrium distribution of molecular systems

nodes.text: Physics-informed diffusion pre-training (PIDP) trains DiG directly from system energy functions (such as force fields) rather than from sampled structures, addressing data-scarce settings.
nodes.evidence: we develop a physics-informed diffusion pre-training (PIDP) method to train DiG with energy functions (such as force fields) of the systems

nodes.text: Unlike static structure predictors such as AlphaFold, which predict a single high-probability structure, DiG aims to sample the full equilibrium distribution including metastable and intermediate states.
nodes.evidence: static structure prediction methods, such as AlphaFold1, aim at predicting one single highprobability structure of a molecule

nodes.text: DiG draws inspiration from simulated annealing and from diffusion processes, gradually transforming a simple distribution into the target equilibrium distribution.
nodes.evidence: DiG draws inspiration from simulated annealing23–26 ... DiG simulates a diffusion process that gradually transforms a simple distribution to the target one

nodes.text: Unlike Boltzmann generators, which create a probability flow from a simple reference state but are hard to generalize across different molecules, DiG is designed to generalize across molecular systems.
nodes.evidence: Boltzmann generators21 are a deep learning approach to generate equilibrium distributions by creating a probability flow from a simple reference state, but this also hard to generalize to different molecules ... We show that DiG can generalize across molecular systems

nodes.text: DiG's per-step independent training signal avoids long-chain back-propagation, enabling efficient training in both data-based and energy-supervised modes.
nodes.evidence: the model gets a training signal in each diffusion step independently ... enabling efficient training that avoids long-chain back-propagation

nodes.text: Because the simple distribution has a closed-form density, DiG enables independent sampling of the equilibrium distribution and provides density estimates, orders of magnitude faster than conventional methods like MD.
nodes.evidence: provides estimations of state densities, orders of magnitude faster than conventional methods

nodes.text: The diffusion process in DiG can be biased toward desired properties, enabling inverse design of molecular structures for properties that lack sufficient training data.
nodes.evidence: The diffusion process can also be biased towards a desired property for inverse design

nodes.text: For SARS-CoV-2 RBD and main protease, whose MD simulation data were not used in training, DiG-generated structures resemble the conformational distributions from millisecond-timescale MD simulations, with about 70% of RBD conformations covered by 10,000 DiG structures.
nodes.evidence: about 70% of the RBD conformations sampled by simulations can be covered with just 10,000 DiG-generated structures

nodes.text: DiG generates multiple experimentally-determined functional states for proteins including adenylate kinase (open/closed, backbone RMSD < 1.0 Angstrom to closed state 1ake), LmrP, human BRAF kinase, and D-ribose binding protein.
nodes.evidence: backbone root mean square difference (r.m.s.d.) < 1.0 Å to the closed state, 1ake

nodes.text: Across 409 held-out protein-ligand systems, DiG-generated ligand conformations had an average RMSD of 1.74 Angstrom to crystal structures, with the best of 50 generated structures within 2.0 Angstrom RMSD for nearly all systems.
nodes.evidence: an r.m.s.d. value of 1.74 Å on average ... The best matched structure among 50 generated structures for each system is within 2.0 Å r.m.s.d. ... for nearly all 409 testing systems

nodes.text: DiG identified some failure cases, notably cluster I conformations of the main protease and RBD that were underrepresented or not recovered, indicating room for improvement.
nodes.evidence: conformations in cluster I are not well recovered by DiG, indicating room for improvement

nodes.text: DiG generalizes more readily than prior approaches such as enhanced sampling (which needs system-specific collective variables) and deep coarse-grained MD (which has not demonstrated generalization).
nodes.evidence: Enhanced sampling simulations14,15 and Markov state modelling16 ... need system-specific collective variables and are not easily generalized ... deep learning coarse-grained methods have worked well for individual molecular systems but have not yet demonstrated generalization
